related_questions.question: What is the best treatment for choriocarcinoma?
related_questions.snippet: Chemotherapy is the most common treatment for an invasive mole or choriocarcinoma. An invasive mole is a cancer that can form in the womb after an abnormal type of pregnancy called a molar pregnancy. It is also called persistent trophoblastic disease (PTD).
related_questions.title: Cancer drug treatment for invasive mole and choriocarcinoma

related_questions.question: What is the survival rate for choriocarcinoma?
related_questions.snippet: Outlook / Prognosis The survival rate for people with high-risk gestational choriocarcinoma is 94%. Non-gestational choriocarcinoma (not related to a prior abnormal pregnancy/placental tissue) has a worse prognosis and is less chemosensitive, which means chemotherapy may not be as effective in killing the cancer cells.
related_questions.title: Choriocarcinoma: Causes, Symptoms, Treatment & Prevention

related_questions.question: How is choriocarcinoma treated in men?
related_questions.snippet: The treatment of choriocarcinoma includes orchidectomy, chemotherapy, and retroperitoneal lymph node dissection. As most cases of choriocarcinoma have poor risk features, primary chemotherapy is followed by radiographic reassessment and staging.
related_questions.title: Testicular Choriocarcinoma Treatment & Management

related_questions.question: What type of cancer is a choriocarcinoma?
related_questions.snippet: Choriocarcinoma is a fast-growing cancer that occurs in a woman's uterus (womb). The abnormal cells start in the tissue that would normally become the placenta. The placenta is the organ that develops during pregnancy to feed the fetus. Choriocarcinoma is a type of gestational trophoblastic disease.

text_blocks.snippet: Choriocarcinoma treatment primarily involves chemotherapy, with surgery and radiation therapy used in some cases, particularly for high-risk or metastatic disease. Chemotherapy is often very effective, with almost 100% survival rates for low-risk cases, according to Cleveland Clinic.
snippet_highlighted_words: chemotherapy, with surgery and radiation therapy used in some cases

list.title: Methotrexate (MTX):
list.snippet: Often the first-line treatment for low-risk choriocarcinoma, but resistance can occur.

list.title: Actinomycin D (Act-D):
list.snippet: Can be used to salvage cases resistant to methotrexate, but more toxic combination chemotherapy might be needed.

list.title: Multi-agent regimens:
list.snippet: For high-risk or metastatic disease, combination chemotherapy is standard. Common regimens include:
EMA-CO: Etoposide, methotrexate, dactinomycin, cyclophosphamide, and vincristine.

list.title: Surgery:
list.snippet: Hysterectomy (removal of the uterus) may be an option, particularly for low-risk cases, to shorten chemotherapy duration. In rare cases, it may be necessary for high-risk patients.

list.title: Radiation Therapy:
list.snippet: May be used in conjunction with chemotherapy for brain metastases or for patients who don't respond to chemotherapy alone.

list.title: Risk Stratification:
list.snippet: Treatment is tailored based on the stage and risk factors of the choriocarcinoma.

list.title: Monitoring:
list.snippet: Regular monitoring of hCG levels is crucial during and after treatment to assess response and detect any recurrence.

list.title: Side Effects:
list.snippet: Chemotherapy can cause side effects, and your healthcare team will provide support and management strategies.
